title: Ghost Engine v1.9.1 is now public — a deterministic state engine for persistent AI/NPC systems
author: GhoCentric
selftext:
I USE AN LLM TO CODE!!!!! I ALSO USE THE LLM TO EXPLAIN MY WORK EASIER!!! 

I am looking for LITERALLY ANY FEEDBACK!!!

I have been using the same llm for three years for this project. I have taken every comment I got on previous reddit posts into consideration. Every. Single. One. I proof read everything and decide whether or not to proceed with whats written. I understand and am aware of the current opinions and frustrations surrounding llms. With that being said, this paragraph is to inform you I use one.

I learn as I step. I run before I walk. So if you don't like llms or think they only produce slop, you have been warned I use one.

Ghost is simply a state machine for emotions/continuous state change. I have finally included a real playable demo(NOT A FINISHED GAME!). 

The game world is basically remembered/used to influence NPCs. Other npcs also influence each other.

I am soon going to add set weights between 0-1(thats the metric I see in my head surrounding the 5 flat layers, stacked on top of each other, that I see in my brain. Thats where they come from) per emotion. 

So like:

Fear: 0.30

Sadness:0.23

Anger:0.65

Ect

The highest number "wins" the internal battle per say but the other lower numbers influence how the winning number is handled. Essentially. 

Now below is the llm written explanation of where I am at:

LLM's explanation based off three years of consecutive work:

"Ghost is a lightweight deterministic state engine designed to sit underneath higher-level AI systems.

It is not a language model and it is not a decision-maker.

Its job is to maintain structured state over time so that systems built on top of it do not have to rely entirely on prompt history or probabilistic model behavior to preserve continuity.

The basic architecture is:

event/input → deterministic state transition → structured state packet → higher-level system response

Ghost currently supports:

\\- persistent relationships

\\- trust and hostility

\\- emotional inertia

\\- temperament

\\- relationship maturity and volatility

\\- social propagation

\\- threat response

\\- governance and policy state

\\- objectives

\\- world state

\\- deterministic scenario/runtime state

\\- snapshot and restore

\\- structured LLM adapter boundaries

\\- epistemic state

\\- observations

\\- claims

\\- evidence

\\- confidence

\\- provenance

\\- belief revision

One of the more important pieces is the epistemic layer.

Ghost does not have to treat a statement such as:

«“The king stole the food.”»

as objective truth.

The engine can keep separate representations for:

what actually happened

what was observed

what somebody claimed happened

what another agent interpreted from that claim

how confident that agent is

what evidence supports the belief

how that belief changes when new evidence appears

That creates a deterministic foundation for systems involving rumors, deception, incomplete information, mistaken interpretation, testimony, faction knowledge, and belief revision.

Ghost Revolution is one of the larger demonstrations built on top of the engine.

It uses Ghost to maintain persistent world and character state while higher-level systems handle gameplay, narration, and LLM reasoning.

The important distinction is that consequences do not have to be invented by the language model.

The state already exists.

The model can reason over it.

The core question behind Ghost is:

How do you give probabilistic AI systems a persistent, deterministic world underneath them?

Instead of asking a model to repeatedly reconstruct what the world probably looks like from context, Ghost maintains the state directly and exposes it in a structured form.

The language model can then focus on interpretation, reasoning, dialogue, and generation without also being responsible for being the database, state machine, relationship system, belief system, and history of the world."

comments.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
comments.body: What makes your system different from all the others?

replies.author: GhoCentric
replies.body:
My response:
I dont have to manually code each state change. I(the llm) codes the state transition rules. 

Also, when using an llm with ghost, the llm doesn't lose continuity. The llm cant make anything up because ghost sends a deterministic packet to the llm to follow along with the prompt from the llm bridge. 

Also zero dependencies. Nothing else is required to be installed to use ghost. You only need tour game world, ghost and an optional llm layer(if ya want AI npcs).

The costs are super low as well. In the available dev shortcut in my pip tool, you can input your own API key(it will be hidden within the terminal) and start the run. The llms being used:

GPT-5.6 Sol → opponent strategy/decision-making, reasoning effort medium

GPT-5.6 Terra → combat + scene narration, reasoning effort none

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Now, here is the LLM recommended response based off my response and three years of accumulated workflow history:

"The biggest difference is that I’m trying to avoid manually scripting every reaction.
You send an event through Ghost’s API, and Ghost deterministically updates the existing state based on the event plus the state that already exists. The game/LLM then reacts to the resulting state instead of me having to hard-code “if player does X, NPC does Y.”

So the same event doesn’t necessarily produce the same behavioral outcome forever, because the NPC/world already has accumulated history.
Ghost also keeps that state persistent and inspectable. Relationships, temperament, threat, social influence, beliefs/evidence, world state, etc. can all evolve over time, be serialized/restored, and be used by whatever system sits on top.

Another big part is that the LLM is not the authority over the world state. It can interpret or narrate, but Ghost owns the deterministic state underneath it.

And with the epistemic layer, even something an NPC says doesn’t automatically become truth. Ghost can separate what actually happened, what was observed, what was claimed, what another NPC believes, how confident they are, and what evidence changes that belief later.

So I guess the short version is: I’m trying to make reactions emerge from accumulated state instead of scripting every reaction individually."

replies.author: GhoCentric
replies.body:
It’s not a hosted API. Ghost is a Python package/state engine that exposes an API developers can call, and yes, it is released already.

I also only post once every few months. I dont think I've posted here before. 

I hope what is below helps you understand what I am doing. 

The main thing I’m trying to do differently is avoid manually scripting every possible NPC reaction while also not letting the LLM own the persistent world state.

For example, instead of coding:

"player insults guard -> guard becomes angry -> guard attacks"

Ghost receives the insult as an event and updates the guard’s existing state based on what is already there: relationship history, trust, hostility, temperament, threat, previous interactions, etc.

So the same insult does not have to produce the same behavioral result every time. The event changes the accumulated state, and whatever sits on top of Ghost uses that resulting state to decide what happens next.

NPCs can also influence each other, so state/history is not limited to player -> NPC interactions.

There is also an epistemic layer that separates things like:

fact -> observation -> claim -> belief -> confidence/evidence

So if one NPC tells another “the player murdered someone,” Ghost does not automatically treat that statement as objective truth. The receiving NPC can believe it with some level of confidence, have evidence/provenance attached to that belief, and revise it later.

The LLM is optional and sits above all of this. It can interpret, reason, choose an intent, or narrate, but Ghost owns the deterministic state underneath it.

So the shortest explanation I can give is:

Instead of authoring every reaction, I’m trying to author the rules of state change once and let reactions emerge from the accumulated state.

If there are existing projects doing this same combination, I genuinely want to see them and compare approaches.
